Expectation1: Conduct experiments to test hypotheses and gather data
Situation1: The experiment can be run on several upcoming dates, and skipping this slot would not disrupt the overall timeline.
Expectation2: Challenge unfair systems and influence policy change
Situation2: They gather recurring cases of unfair treatment and bring them to discussions with community leaders or officials.
Story: I stared at my calendar, the lab schedule open on one screen, and a draft of my advocacy report on the other. As a scientist, I was expected to run the next phase of my experiment—an intricate setup that could be rescheduled, but only at the cost of losing momentum. My advisor trusted me to keep the project moving, and my team relied on my data. Yet, as an advocate, I had promised to attend a crucial meeting with community leaders, where I was to present evidence of recurring injustices faced by marginalized groups. The meeting was set for the same afternoon as my experiment slot. The community counted on me to give voice to their struggles, to push for real change. I felt the weight of both worlds pressing in—one demanding objectivity and precision, the other passion and presence. My mind raced with the possible consequences of letting either side down, torn between the pursuit of knowledge and the pursuit of justice, knowing that whatever I chose, something important would be left behind.
